title: Lookup and one-time handoff
summary: A customer calls the CRM, is found by phone, and is handed to the ERP with a one-time identifier. The two systems end up with two different, unlinkable pseudonyms for the same person.

steps.label: CRM registers the contact
steps.note: The agent captures name, email, phone and a loyalty tier. Sunder normalizes the identifiers, stores everything encrypted in the CRM's own scope, and returns a stable pseudonym (CID). Nothing searchable by PII lands in the CRM database.

steps.label: Agent looks her up by phone - hit
steps.note: The agent types the number from caller ID. Sunder HMAC-tokenizes it and matches against the token index: no plaintext identifier is compared or stored on this path, and the lookup lands in the audit chain. LOOKUP != AUTHENTICATION - a hit never proves the caller is that person.

assert.message: The lookup returned the same pseudonym as the registration - the agent found the right record.

steps.label: Read one field, with a stated purpose
steps.note: Field-level access: exactly one decrypted value, only under a purpose this client is allowed to use (here: support), and the read is audited. There is no endpoint that returns the whole record.

steps.label: Lookup by name alone is refused
steps.note: A name is a narrowing key, never an identifier. 'Find me every Ana Horvat' is exactly the enumeration a breached CRM enables today, so it is a 400 - a name only works as a second factor next to an email or a phone.

steps.label: A miss is a 404, and it is counted
steps.note: An unknown identifier returns 404 not_found. Every miss is audited and feeds the enumeration detector (alert and metric at 100 misses in 10 minutes); past the per-client rate limit the answer becomes 429.

steps.label: CRM issues a one-time identifier for the ERP
steps.note: The order has to move to the ERP, but the CRM's pseudonym must not cross the scope boundary. The CRM asks for a one-time identifier: five minutes, one use, one audience (erp), one purpose (create_order).

steps.label: ERP redeems it and gets its OWN pseudonym
steps.note: The ERP receives a CID in the ERP scope. Two different pseudonyms for the same person: neither system can join its records against the other's, even if both databases leak. The issuer never learns the ERP's CID.

assert.message: The two systems hold different pseudonyms - the leaked databases would not correlate.

steps.label: Replaying the token is a 409
steps.note: Single use is an atomic VALID -> USED database transition, not just a signature check: the second redemption of the same token fails even if the signature is perfect.
